subject: Agriculture
title: Chickens from the Jungle
description: One-minute skill: Chickens from the Jungle.

hook.text: Every chicken on earth descends from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia. There are now 33 billion of them.

buildup.text: Junglefowl were likely first kept not for food but for cockfighting. Eggs and meat came later.

discovery.text: Chickens spread along trade routes—from Asia to Egypt to Rome. They were easy to transport and bred fast.

twist.text: Wild junglefowl lay about 12 eggs per year. Modern hens lay over 300. Breeding reshaped their biology.

climax.text: Chickens are now the world's most numerous bird—outnumbering all wild birds combined.

punchline.text: A jungle bird became the planet's most common animal.

quiz.question: How many eggs does a wild junglefowl lay per year compared to a modern hen?

details.summary: Domestic chickens descend from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, domesticated at least 3,000–4,000 years ago. This topic traces how a shy tropical bird became the most numerous livestock animal on Earth, with over 30 billion alive at any given time.
details.whyItMatters: Chickens provide the cheapest animal protein worldwide. Their rapid reproduction, small size, and adaptability make them the most accessible livestock for smallholder farmers and industrial producers alike.
takeaways: Domestic chickens descend primarily from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia
There are over 30 billion chickens alive at any given moment globally
Chickens were initially domesticated for cockfighting, not food production

faq.question: Where and when were chickens first domesticated?
faq.answer: Recent research points to rice-farming communities in Southeast Asia around 1500 BCE domesticating the red junglefowl (Gallus gallus). Earlier claims of 8,000-year-old domestication have been challenged by newer archaeological and genetic evidence.

faq.question: Why were chickens originally domesticated?
faq.answer: Evidence suggests chickens were first kept for cockfighting and ceremonial purposes rather than food. Their role as a primary protein source developed gradually as they spread from Southeast Asia to China, India, the Middle East, and eventually worldwide.
